postTitle: Moving Countries: Rebuilding Your Financial Identity
topic: A transfer with no fee can still cost money in the exchange rate

assumptions.notes: Reel's own example, illustrative: €300 sent with no transfer fee; the provider's exchange rate costs €6 (2%), so €294 worth arrives. The lesson's figures: about 6.5% global average cost, about 2% at some digital providers.

hookVariants.narration: You send three hundred euros home with no transfer fee. Could changing currencies still cost you?
onscreenLines: You send €300 home with no transfer fee
Could changing currencies still cost you?

beats.narration: At the market's exchange price, that buys three hundred euros' worth of the other currency.
The provider offers less currency for your money.
That difference costs six euros in this example.
So two hundred ninety four euros' worth arrives, despite no transfer fee.

cta.narration: Send this to someone who sends money home.
cta.subtext: No fee can still mean a cost

caption.instagram:
You send €300 home with no transfer fee. Could changing currencies still cost you?

Yes. A transfer has two costs, and only one is shown. The fee is the visible one. The other sits in the exchange rate: the provider gives a little less currency for the money than the market price. In this example that gap costs €6, so €294 worth arrives.

The comparison that captures both is how much the person at the other end receives for a fixed amount sent. The cost also depends on the route: busy routes with many providers tend to be cheap, thin ones expensive. The World Bank puts the global average cost near 6.5% of the amount sent.
